title: Four stages
hook: stream-enterer, once-returner, non-returner, arahant: the Theravada map

segments.voice: Yesterday: noting, and your line, rising, falling: a soft name for each moment.

Hikers on a long trail carry a map. It shows the passes, the rivers, the campsites, roughly where you'll be after a week. On a foggy day it's enormously useful. But picture a hiker who spends the whole walk staring at it, comparing his dot to everyone else's, bragging at each campsite about how far he's come. He's missed the mountains. The Theravada tradition has a map of the whole path to awakening: four stages, each with a name, one of the oldest maps in Buddhism. And it comes with some firm rules about how not to use it.
screen: `A MAP ON A LONG TRAIL.` → `STARING AT THE DOT.` → `FOUR STAGES, FIRM RULES.`

segments.voice: The suttas describe the path as cutting ten fetters, ten ropes that tie the mind. Four stages mark the way. First, the stream-enterer, sotāpanna. Three fetters fall: belief in a fixed self, doubt about the path, and clinging to rites as if they alone could save you. The stream now flows toward awakening; the texts say at most seven more lives. More on that tomorrow. Second, the once-returner, sakadāgāmī: greed and ill will grow thin. At most one more human life. Third, the non-returner, anāgāmī: sensual craving and ill will are gone completely. No return to this world. Fourth, the arahant, the worthy one: the last five fetters fall, down to conceit, restlessness and ignorance. Fully awake, free, nothing more to do. Each stage has two moments, the path and its fruit, so Theravada Buddhists chant about the noble community as four pairs of persons, eight kinds of individuals. Now the rules. A monk who falsely claims any of these attainments commits one of the four defeats from four days ago and is no longer a monk. A monk who truly has one isn't supposed to announce it to lay people either; that's an offense too. So the map is for finding your way, not for ranking yourself or anyone else. Mahayana schools teach a different map, the bodhisattva's path you met in the Heart Sutra; each tradition describes its own way and its own goal. The Theravada map says where the trail goes. It doesn't keep score.
screen: `TEN FETTERS, FOUR STAGES.` · `STREAM-ENTERER, ONCE-RETURNER.` · `NON-RETURNER, ARAHANT.` · `NO BRAGGING, BY RULE.` · then, large: `A MAP, NOT A SCOREBOARD.`

segments.voice: Say the four names slowly, one per breath: stream-enterer, once-returner, non-returner, arahant. If the mind asks, where am I on this?, see that wanting, and set it down gently. Fold the map into your pocket and come back to this breath, this body, the ground under you.
Four stages. Stream-enterer, once-returner, non-returner, arahant: the Theravada map of awakening, fetter by fetter.
Your line: a map, not a scoreboard. The view matters more than the dot. That's day two hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: Theravada Buddhists chant the qualities of the noble community, 'four pairs of persons, eight kinds of individuals', in daily devotions; by monastic rule, monks don't announce their own attainments to lay people.

fork.setup: a friend on retreat whispers that he thinks he's become a stream-enterer and wants to post about it. what does the Theravada tradition's attitude suggest?
options: post it; progress should be celebrated.
keep it quiet; the map is for finding your way, not ranking.
ask everyone else what stage they're at.
fork.reveal: monastic rules forbid claiming attainments, falsely or even truly, to lay people; the stages are a map, not a scoreboard.

original.note: Pali ariyapuggala: noble person, anyone who has reached one of the four stages.

trapdoor: what you thought: the four stages are ranks, like belts in karate.
what it means: a map of fetters falling away, meant for finding the way, not for keeping score.
what a scholar hears: falsely claiming a 'superhuman state' is the fourth pārājika, and truthfully telling a lay person is pācittiya 8; the ten fetters are listed in suttas such as AN 10.13.
